## Prep work

```{r,message=F,warning=FALSE,echo=T, eval=T}
library(tidyverse)
library(kableExtra) # for formatting in presentation; optional
library(maps) # for map example
library(plotly) # for interactive plot
```

## Tidy data

"Tidy data sets are all alike; but every messy data set is messy in its own way." - Hadley Wickham

```{r, echo=T, eval=T}
head(airquality)
```

Important features:

- Each **variable** is in its own **column**
- Each **observation** is in its own **row**
- Each value is in its own cell

Datasets with these features are referred to as "tidy data" (or "long data"). Most functions in R (esp. in the **tidyverse** packages) expect your data to be in the tidy format.

Tidy data is not a mathematically defined concept; *the best way to format data is subjective and based on the goal of the project*.

kable(table4a);kable(table4b)

What can we do to improve the format of this data?

## Convert wide data into long data
```{r, echo=T, eval=T}
table4a
table4a %>% pivot_longer(cols = 2:3, 
            names_to = "year", 
            values_to = "case.number")
```

- Two new columns are created ('year' and 'case.number')
- The new column named by **names_to** contains old column names
- The new column named by **values_to** contains old cell values
- Columns 2 and 3 in the old data are "stacked"

Exercise: convert **table4b** to the following format

```{r,echo=T}
#| code-fold: true  
#| code-summary: "Show code"
pivot_longer(table4b, cols = 2:3, names_to = "year", values_to = "population")
```


## Example: exam scores

Run the following code to create a data frame of exam scores. What would the long format look like? Use R to convert it to the long format and call it **df.score.long**.

```{r,echo=T}
df.score <- data.frame(student = c('A','B','C'),
                   math = c(99,73,12),
                   literature = c(45,78,96),
                   PE = c(56, 55, 57))
df.score
```

<details>

<summary>Solution</summary>

```{r,eval=T,echo=T}
df.score.long <- df.score %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = 2:4, names_to = "subject", values_to = "score")
df.score.long
```

</details>

<details>

<summary>Different ways to specify the columns you want to stack</summary>

```{r,echo=T,eval=F}
# these code are equivalent 
df.score %>% pivot_longer(cols = 2:4, names_to = "subject", values_to = "score")
df.score %>% pivot_longer(cols = c(math,literature,PE), names_to = "subject", values_to = "score")
df.score %>% pivot_longer(cols = math:PE, names_to = "subject", values_to = "score")
df.score %>% pivot_longer(cols = -student, names_to = "subject", values_to = "score")
```

</details>

## But why?

As an example, try generating the following graphs with **df.score**, and then with **df.score.long**. Which format is easier?

```{r,fig.height=3,fig.width=6,out.width="100%",echo=F}
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
boxplot(df.score.long$score ~ df.score.long$student, xlab='students', ylab='scores') 
boxplot(df.score.long$score ~ df.score.long$subject, xlab='subjects', ylab='scores') 
```

<details>

<summary>Sample code</summary>

```{r,eval=F,echo=T}
# --------------------------------------------------- #
# Long format: code for both graphs are very similar
# --------------------------------------------------- #
boxplot(df.score.long$score ~ df.score.long$student, 
        xlab='students', 
        ylab='scores')
# OR #
df.score.long %>% ggplot(aes(x=student, y=score)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_minimal()

boxplot(df.score.long$score ~ df.score.long$subject, 
        xlab='subjects', 
        ylab='scores')
# OR #
df.score.long %>% ggplot(aes(x=subject, y=score)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_minimal()


# --------------------------------------------------- #
# Short format: not easy with ggplot; base R coding is not unified
# --------------------------------------------------- #
boxplot(as.numeric(df.score[1,2:4]),
        as.numeric(df.score[2,2:4]),
        as.numeric(df.score[3,2:4]))

boxplot(df.score$math,df.score$literature,df.score$PE)
```

</details>

## Convert long data into wide data

```{r,echo=T,eval=T}
df.score.long
df.score.long %>% pivot_wider(names_from=subject, values_from=score)
```

- **subject** and **score** are not put in quotation, as they refer to **existing** columns in the dataset
- Variable specified by **names_from** becomes new column names; this variable has $3$ unique values, so $3$ new columns are created
- Variable specified by **values_from** becomes new cell values

# Map

## maps package

```{r,eval=T,echo=T}
library(maps)
# there are a few different maps included in this package
# see ?map_data

mymap <- map_data(map="state")
```

What exactly is **mymap**? Try some information extraction/visualization

```{r,eval=T,echo=T}
plot(mymap$long,mymap$lat)

ggplot(data=mymap,aes(x=long,y=lat,group=group)) +
  geom_polygon() +
  coord_fixed(1.4) +
  theme_void()
```

## New Jersey map by county

```{r,eval=T, out.width='20%', echo=T}
mymap <- map_data(map="county") %>%
    filter(region == 'new jersey')

## NJ County map ##
mymap %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=long,y=lat,group=group)) +
  geom_polygon(fill='lightblue',color='darkblue') +
  coord_fixed(1.4) +
  theme_void()
```

## New Jersey data

- Download the [**NJ_county.csv**](../../../../dataset/NJ_county.csv) dataset and import to R (scraped from [wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_New_Jersey_locations_by_per_capita_income))

```{r}
df.nj <- read.csv("../../../../dataset/NJ_county.csv")
str(df.nj)
```

## Combine data

We want to combine these two existing data:

```{r, echo=T}
df.nj %>% slice_head(n=3)

mymap %>% slice_head(n=3)
```

- We need to match **County** with **subregion**
- We need to make sure the county spellings are consistent (e.g., all lower case)

## 
```{r, echo=T}
# convert county name to lower case
df.nj$County <- tolower(df.nj$County)

# combine data
mymap.nj <- left_join(mymap, df.nj, by=c('subregion'='County'))

mymap.nj %>% slice_head(n=3)
```

## Visualization!

Now we can do all the fun stuff like visualizing a map. Also, note here that you can store a ggplot like a regular R object. This is *not* the case with base R plots.

```{r, eval=T, echo=T}
p1 <- mymap.nj %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=long,y=lat,group=group,fill=Per_capita_income,text=subregion)) +
  geom_polygon(color='darkblue') +
  coord_fixed(1.4) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(fill='Per capita income') +
  scale_fill_gradient(low="yellow", high="blue")
p1
```

## Interactive map with county names
We set **text=subregion** in the previous ggplot. The goal is to show the county names on the map as text. This is very easy with an **interactive** graph: the **ggplotly( )** function in the **plotly** package allows you to convert an existing ggplot to an interactive version.

```{r,eval=T , echo=T}
ggplotly(p1)
```

## 
To do the same graph with non-interactive ggplot is not as easy, since you have to specify exactly *where* to put each of the text.

<details>

<summary>Sample code</summary>

```{r,eval=T,echo=T}
# calculate average longitude and latitude for text coordinate
county_labels <- mymap.nj %>%
  group_by(subregion) %>%
  summarize(
    long = mean(long),
    lat = mean(lat),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# add text
p1 +
  geom_text(data = county_labels, 
            aes(x = long, y = lat, label = subregion),
            inherit.aes = FALSE,
            size = 2)
  

```

</details>

## Different ways to join data

Exercise:

1.  Create the following data frames:

```{r,echo=T}
df.student <- 
  data.frame(name=c('A','B','C','D'),
             exam=c(80,91,85,78),
             project=c(1,2,1,NA))

df.project <-
  data.frame(projectID = c(1:3),
             description = c('visualization','classification','text mining'))
```

```{r,echo=T}
df.student
df.project
```


2.  Run **?left_join()** to understand different ways to join data. Think about what each line of the following code should return. Run each line to confirm.

```{r,echo=T,eval=F}
inner_join(df.student, df.project, by=c('project' = 'projectID'))
left_join(df.student, df.project, by=c('project' = 'projectID'))
left_join(df.project, df.student, by=c('projectID' = 'project'))
right_join(df.student, df.project, by=c('project' = 'projectID'))
full_join(df.student, df.project, by=c('project' = 'projectID'))
```
